title: Review: Electronegativity, polarity and intermolecular forces; Giant covalent structures; Oxidation states and naming
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: RX02#t3 term and clue written for the game; RX02#t2 term and clue written for the game; BD04#t1 term and clue written for the game; BD04#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BD04#N.12a, BD05#N.7, RX02#N.10, BD04#N.2a, BD05#N.11a, RX02#N.4a, BD04#N.4a, RX02#N.9, BD04#N.7a, RX02#N.8, BD04#N.14, BD04#N.9a. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Metal hydride
items.clue: Compound such as NaH or CaH₂ in which H is −1.

items.label: Peroxide
items.clue: Compound such as H₂O₂ or Na₂O₂ in which O is −1.

items.label: Electronegativity
items.clue: The ability of an atom to attract the bonding pair in a covalent bond.

items.label: London forces
items.clue: Electron movement makes a temporary dipole that induces one in a nearby molecule.

questions.stem: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, mixes with water in all proportions, but hexane, C₆H₁₄, does not dissolve in water. Which statement explains this difference?

options.text: Ethanol splits into ions that water surrounds, but hexane does not form ions
Ethanol can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, but hexane cannot
Hexane is less dense than water, so it floats on the water rather than dissolving
Hexane molecules are too large to fit into the gaps between water molecules

questions.explanation: Ethanol's O–H hydrogen bonds to water, replacing the ones broken. Hexane offers only weak London forces.

questions.stem: Substance X melts at 1710 °C. It does not conduct electricity, either as a solid or when molten. It does not dissolve in water or in hexane. Which structure does X have?

options.text: A lattice of oppositely charged ions
A network of atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout
A lattice of metal cations in a sea of delocalised electrons
Separate small molecules with very strong forces between them

questions.explanation: The very high melting point means strong bonds break. No conduction even when molten means no ions and no delocalised electrons. Insoluble everywhere: a covalent network.

questions.stem: Chlorine is −1 in the chloride ion, Cl⁻, but +1 in the hypochlorite ion, ClO⁻ (in bleach). Which explains the +1?

options.text: The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ has lost a proton to the oxygen atom, leaving chlorine with a +1 charge.
Oxygen always has the oxidation number −1 in an ion with one negative charge.
Oxygen is more electronegative than chlorine, so it is assigned the shared electrons in the Cl–O bond.
The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ carries a real charge of +1, as in a Cl⁺ ion.

questions.explanation: O takes both shared electrons and is −2; the total must be −1, so x + (−2) = −1 and Cl is +1. In Cl⁻, chlorine holds an extra electron: −1.

questions.stem: Electronegativity values: H 2.2, C 2.6, O 3.4, F 4.0, P 2.2. Which bond is the most polar?

options.text: O–H
O–F
C–F
P–H

questions.explanation: 4.0 − 2.6 = 1.4, the largest difference, so the pair is pulled most towards F.

questions.stem: Graphite conducts electricity far better along its layers than at right angles to them. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Its layers slide over each other, and charge is carried only in the direction they slide.
Its ions lie between the layers, so they can move only in the plane of the layers.
Each atom forms four bonds within its layer, so no electrons are left to pass between layers.
Its delocalised electrons move freely within a layer, but cannot easily cross the gap to the next.

questions.explanation: Each C bonds to three others; its fourth electron is delocalised over its own layer only. So charge flows easily along a layer, but hardly between layers.

questions.stem: What are the oxidation numbers of hydrogen in sodium hydride, NaH, and of oxygen in sodium peroxide, Na₂O₂?
questions.explanation: In NaH, Na is +1, so H is −1 (the hydride ion). In Na₂O₂, 2(+1) + 2x = 0, so O is −1 (the peroxide ion, O₂²⁻).

questions.stem: Water, H₂O, is a polar molecule with a permanent dipole (electronegativity: H 2.2, O 3.4). Which statement explains this?

options.text: Its O–H bonds are polar, and every molecule with polar bonds has a permanent dipole
It is bent, so its two O–H bond dipoles do not point in opposite directions
Its H atoms lie at 90° to each other, as in its dot-and-cross diagram, so the dipoles add
Its oxygen atom has two lone pairs, which are the only source of its permanent dipole

questions.explanation: Each O–H is δ− at O. At about 104.5° the two dipoles add to a resultant.

questions.stem: What is the formula of sodium chlorate(III)?

options.text: NaClO₃
Na₃ClO
NaCl₃O
NaClO₂

questions.explanation: In ClO₂⁻, x + 2(−2) = −1, so Cl = +3. One Na⁺ balances the 1− charge.

questions.stem: Liquid methanol, CH₃OH, contains hydrogen bonds. What is a hydrogen bond in methanol?

options.text: An attraction between the H of an O–H group and a lone pair on O in another molecule
The covalent bond between the O atom and the H atom within one methanol molecule
An attraction between the H atoms of one molecule and the H atoms of another
An attraction between an H atom of the CH₃ group and an O atom in a neighbouring molecule

questions.explanation: H bonded to O is δ+, and it is attracted to a lone pair on the O of a neighbour.

options.text: K₂Cr₂O₇, potassium dichromate(VI)
K₂MnO₄, potassium manganate(IV)
Fe₂(SO₄)₃, iron(VI) sulfate
MnCl₂, manganese(VII) chloride

questions.explanation: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0 gives 2x = +12, so each Cr is +6. The numeral is per atom.

questions.stem: Ammonia, NH₃ (Mᵣ 17.0), boils at −33 °C. Phosphine, PH₃ (Mᵣ 34.0), boils at −88 °C. Electronegativity: H 2.2, N 3.0, P 2.2. Why does the lighter molecule boil higher?

options.text: PH₃ molecules have no forces between them, because their P–H bonds are non-polar.
NH₃ has stronger London forces than PH₃, because it is the smaller molecule.
NH₃ molecules hydrogen bond to each other; PH₃ molecules cannot.
Boiling NH₃ breaks its N–H bonds, which are stronger than P–H bonds.

questions.explanation: N is very electronegative, so N–H is δ+ at H, and each N has a lone pair: N–H⋯N hydrogen bonds. P–H bonds are hardly polar (both 2.2), so PH₃ has no hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: Propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃ (Mᵣ 44.11), ethanal, CH₃CHO (Mᵣ 44.06), and ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH (Mᵣ 46.08), have comparable molar masses. Which lists them in order of increasing boiling point?

options.text: propane < ethanal < ethanol
propane < ethanol < ethanal
ethanal < propane < ethanol
ethanal < ethanol < propane

questions.explanation: Similar masses, so the force type decides: London only (−42 °C), dipole–dipole added (20 °C), hydrogen bonds (78 °C).
